# How to play

One button, one bubble, and the whole future off to the right. Everything below is detail â honestly, you could close this now and just play. Come back when something bites you.

## The one button

Press and hold â the SPACE BAR , the DOWN ARROW , a mouse button, or a finger held anywhere on the screen â and your bubble turns heavy and drops. Let go and it floats back up. That's the entire control scheme. I promise there is no hidden second button.

The trick is to ride the hills the way a skier would: hold on the way down a slope to gather speed, let go just before the bottom, and the next slope throws you into the sky. Land gently on a downhill slope â moving the way it tilts â and you'll hear a chime. Keep landing like that and the chimes climb a scale, your EXUBERANCE multiplier grows (up to Ã9.9), and the game quietly starts to sing. This takes about three runs to find, and it's worth all three. A smaller pleasure while you practice: skim just above a hillside without touching it, and the game pays you a little +â¥ for the nerve.

One rule worth holding onto: floating and gliding can never hurt you. Diving can â hold all the way into the ground and the bubble cracks. So does a bite from a risk you ignored. Three cracks end the run (five in gentle mode). So when in doubt, do nothing. Surprisingly good advice, in the game and in general.

## What the numbers mean

The YEAR is how far you've come â it's the score. The pink bar is HUMAN FLOURISHING , and it's really the whole game: it leaks away as the pace of change rises, and it refills when you look after the things you meet (watch for the +â¥ signs). If it empties, the lights go out. Push it past 100 and the future starts blooming â literally: flowers appear, and every flower you ever grow joins the meadow on the title screen, forever.

PACE only ever climbs on its own. That's not a flaw â that's the thesis. But you can push back: hold SHIFT , or rest two fingers on the screen, and the world slows down on purpose â the kind of pause people take together when a technology is moving faster than the questions. You'll see it: SLOWING DOWN TO THINK spreads across the sky. Time slows so you can look around, the pace of change genuinely drops and stays dropped for a good while, the hype cools off, and the things that bite bite softer â because this time, you saw them coming. It costs flourishing the whole time you hold it, because thinking time isn't free. It's still the best deal in the game.

And mind the dashed line high in the sky â the hype line. Soar above it and the bubble inflates: bigger, floatier, more fragile, and flourishing drains fast up there. Stay too long and it pops, and nothing will have burst the bubble but the bubble.

## The things you'll meet

The wide-eyed blobs are orphan risks â risks nobody has claimed yet. Hold your button as you roll past one and you adopt it: it gets a name, trails behind you like a duckling, and will one day take a hit meant for you. Fly past it instead and it burrows underground... then returns a few hills later with teeth. That's a bite : it knocks the bubble like a crash, takes a real chunk of flourishing, and the end-of-run card will tell you exactly what it took: trust, dignity, the quiet. From era 4, some blobs carry cameras or antennas â nastier than the plain ones if ignored, but adopt them and the paparazzo's flash starts defending you, and the trending one lends you a permanent tailwind. Keep eight pets, and adopting a ninth graduates your eldest, with a gift.

The scribbly fires are moral panics, and attention is their fuel. Touch one and it flares up and comes after you. Fly past without touching and it dies down on its own â and flourishing grows a little. Three of them marching together is a mob. Never hug a mob.

The diamond signs are risks with names â DEEPFAKE SCANDAL, DATA BREACH, and friends. Hold your button at the moment you hit one and you've managed it (+â¥). Coast into it slack-thumbed and it costs you dearly. Or fly over it entirely, if you can.

The crates are emerging technologies. Catch one and a five-second timer starts; when it runs out, the technology deploys wherever you happen to be â so where you are is the decision . On the ground: tech for good â flowers, +â¥â¥. Above the hype line: RUSHED TO MARKET â a burst of speed and a year gained now, new problems hatching downstream. Some of these technologies are real, some are almost real, and some are nonsense. I'm not telling you which is which. Being unsure is the point.

The golden ? is serendipity. Touch it and something good happens. Never the same thing twice.

The grey sludge pools in the deepest valleys, drags at your speed, and eats flourishing while you wade. Build speed and fly over the top of it.

And from era 5, the black swans : two honks, and then it's on you. A pet will throw itself in the way, if you have one. Pass close by without touching, and the near miss pays two full years.

## The long game

Medals arrive at 10, 25, 50, 100, and 250 hills: DISRUPTION, AWARENESS, AGILITY, RESILIENCE, DIGNITY. The last one is worth seeing.

Survive long enough and the world itself turns â the colors, the board, the doodles, the music â through THE AGE OF DEEP WATER, THE LONG DUSK, and THE AGE OF STRANGE LIGHTS. Past year 3000, arrive at any century still flourishing and a door opens to the post-scarcity future: the drain stops, the panics retire, and only the ground still counts. Records earned there wear â¿. And the story does have an ending â a good one, at year 4000. Bring everything you have grown.

## Today's future

Press T (or tap the purple band on the title screen) and you'll play TODAY'S FUTURE â the identical future everyone in the world is playing today, under the same name. Your daily best is kept separately, and the end-of-run card grows a copy chip, for comparing results with people you enjoy arguing with.

## The quiet stuff (mild spoilers)

A towel waits at hill 42. A quantum duck stands near year 2120 â est. 2020, off by a century on purpose. A robot starts waving around 2057 and does not stop; you will see it again. Somewhere in the mid-2100s, reality resyncs â it is almost certainly nothing. Somewhere in the 2400s, a very large ship passes, very politely; fly up and say hello. In some year ending in 42, against considerable odds: a whale, and some petunias. The century banners tell a long story about jetpacks â it ends in forgiveness. Tap the sun three times and the future gets friendlier: the sun smiles, and your records wear â, because honesty is mandatory. Leave the title screen alone for 22 seconds and someone waves at you. In the AI era, some of the background doodles are pencils, drawing the world. And there is always a coffee ring on the whiteboard. There has to be.

The world has lately grown more small things, and it would be wrong to list them all. But: the weather is occasionally sheep. Or kites, going the wrong way. It varies. There is a playground every century or three, always built a little differently, because there is always a playground. An orange tree grows a long way from home, and once in a while there's a jar. A dish listens. A reader turns the page only if you pass slowly enough to deserve it. A tower on a hill is passing a name on, and always will be. The duck, it turns out, remembers you â across runs, out of order. And somewhere out there is a photographer nobody ever sees, whose photographs turn up later, where the flowers are.

This generation of the game also keeps a small pool of wonders â a bench, a cold pool, a man in a white suit, an elephant made of leaves, and a handful more. At most one appears per run, and most runs carry none, so meeting one means something. The weather has private moods too. And if you do nothing at all for twelve seconds, the game notices, kindly. That's all you're getting from me â some things are better found than told.

# The ideas behind HYPERBUBBLE

HYPERBUBBLE is a one-button game that's inspired by navigating powerful new technologies in a complex world while ensuring future human flourishing. It's designed to be simple to play while sparking curiosity, experimentation and wonder (and you'll need all three to get the most out of it). Devised and coded by Claude Fable 5, and based on the work, thinking, and initiatives of ASU Professor of Advanced Technology Transitions Andrew Maynard.

## A quick note on the game's genesis from Andrew Maynard

HYPERBUBBLE started as an idle moment of speculation while I was exploring Anthropic's Fable 5 AI model. I was in between more complex (and serious) projects, and maximizing use of Fable before my access ran out. Wanting to test its capabilities in coding a simple web-based game, I asked it to research my work and come up with something inspired by it that was simple, fun, and with gameplay that kept you coming back.

HYPERBUBBLE is the result. In some ways it's nothing special â the world is overflowing with simple AI-generated games. What was interesting to me though was the process, and how the game taps into my work in very specific ways. It also provides some insight into how Fable 5 works. Plus, I must confess to loving the game!

After my initial request, Fable did a deep research dive into my work, created five game-designer agents to come up with different concepts, passed these through a panel of three AI judges, and selected the winning (AI-generated) proposal.

After the first draft â which Fable debugged, tested, and checked using an impressive array of sub-agents â it began working earnestly with me to come up with the final product, refining the goals, gameplay, and feel along the way. This resulted in version 1.0 of the game and represented over 20 iterations.

Version 1.0 was originally published on July 10 and featured on the Future of Being Human Substack . However, not content to leave things as they were, I then started to work in earnest with Fable on a version 2.0 that expanded the gameplay substantially, and the ideas and experiences that a player encounters, and then progressed to a version 3.0!

The game is now on version 5 and is considerably more mature than that first iteration, even down to having a leaderboard. It represents over 90 iterations of the initial html file that Fable produced, and has a far greater steer from me than version 1.0 did. However, the fundamentals and implementation still belong to the sometimes-quirky and often unexpected "creative mind" of Fable 5.

That said, the game is intentionally simple. And there are many aspects of it that are still begging to be tweaked and refined. But it still brings a smile to my face every time I play :)
